summary: Reports measurements of FTP user and server programs taken over about six months. It covers the measurement criteria and tools, the results, how they compare with other data, and asks readers for suggestions on the measurement and summary methods.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 573 reports measurements of FTP transfers and host availability collected by MIT-DMS. Its results compare transfer modes and identify implementation choices that could affect speed and processing cost.

questions: how fast was early arpanet file transfer
what ftp transfer measurements did rfc 573 report
how did image 36 compare with ascii 8
subtitle: Measurements of FTP transfer speed, processing cost and reliability.

tldr.problem: The author wanted measured results for FTP performance and a way to compare different transfer modes and costs.
tldr.mechanism: MIT-DMS recorded transfer details in its CALICO system and summarized 304 files, alongside host availability measurements from its SURVEY program.
tldr.outcome: The measurements reported higher average speed and lower processing cost for Image-36 than ASCII-8 transfers, and the author recommended using Image-36 between PDP-10 systems where possible.

today: RFC 573 is a historical report of FTP and host measurements collected by MIT-DMS in 1973.

sections.title: What the Measurements Cover
sections.content: The RFC lists six useful measures for a data-transfer service: transfer rate, response time, processing cost, time between connection failures, availability and accuracy. MIT-DMS's SURVEY program measured response time, failure-to-connect rate and availability for host logger services. The author notes these results are a proxy for FTP service behavior, not a direct measurement of every FTP server.
sections.plainLanguage: The report measures speed, delay, processing effort, connection failures, availability and transfer accuracy. Some results come from host logger checks, which the author treats as an indication of FTP availability.

sections.title: How MIT-DMS Collected Transfer Data
sections.content:
The CALICO FTP user and server recorded each transfer's remote host, time, bit count, elapsed time, CPU time, direction and FTP settings. The record covered byte size, representation type, transfer mode and file structure. The measurements did not include transfers made with non-CALICO FTP programs, so they covered only part of MIT-DMS's FTP use.

The report cautions that SURVEY checked hosts only once every twenty minutes and could not distinguish failures in a host, IMP or telephone line.
sections.plainLanguage: CALICO kept a record of each transfer, including its size, duration, computer cost and settings. The data did not cover all FTP use, and host checks could not identify which part of the network caused a failure.

sections.title: Transfer Results
sections.content:
The measurement system recorded 304 files totaling 57.6 million bits. The table reports an average speed of 7.56 Kbps overall, 9.35 Kbps for Image-36 mode and 2.09 Kbps for ASCII-8 mode. CPU use was 3 seconds per megabit for Image-36 and 19 seconds per megabit for ASCII-8. The highest recorded rate was 27.8 Kbps.

The RFC reports no data-loss problems in its measured transfers and describes transfers of a complete operating-system listing of about 6 million bits that were reassembled and run successfully.
sections.plainLanguage: In this data set, Image-36 transfers were faster and used less CPU time per megabit than ASCII-8 transfers. The author reports that the measured transfers had not revealed data loss.

sections.title: Interpretation and Recommendations
sections.content: The author says transfer speed varied with mode, host load, file size and buffer or allocation sizes. The RFC recommends Image-36 for transfers between PDP-10 systems where possible and asks protocol and program designers to support it for other kinds of transfer too. The author also invites suggestions about the measurements and the way results are summarized.
sections.plainLanguage: The report links transfer performance to the selected mode and the resources available to the programs. It recommends Image-36 for suitable PDP-10 transfers and asks readers to comment on the measurement approach.
